Research Paper
Enhancing mesophilic methanogenesis in oleate-rich environments through 
optimized micro-aeration pretreatment
Xiang Li a, Yi-Juan Yan a, Hong-Ming Wu a, Samir Ibrahim Gadow b, Hongyu Jiang c, Zhe Kong d,  
Yong Hu a,*
a School of Environmental Science and Engineering, Nanjing Tech University, Nanjing 211816, China
b Department of Agricultural Microbiology, Agriculture and Biology Research Institute, National Research Centre, 33 EI Buhouth St., Dokki 12622, Cairo, Egypt
c Beijing Enterprises Water (China) Investment Co., Ltd, BEWG Building, District 7, Wangjing East Park, Chaoyang District, Beijing 100015, China
d School of Environmental Science and Engineering, Suzhou University of Science and Technology, Suzhou 215009, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Micro-aeration pretreatment
Anaerobic digestion
Lipid-rich environment
Methanogenesis pathway
Microbial composition
A B S T R A C T
Micro-aeration pretreatment has emerged as a promising technology for improving the performance of anaerobic 
bioreactors in the treatment of lipid-rich organic waste, particularly in mitigating the accumulation of long-chain 
fatty acids (LCFAs). Micro-aeration intensity is a critical factor in optimizing substrate hydrolysis and meth­
anogenesis efficiency. In this study, optimal micro-aeration intensities for acetoclastic (30 mL-air/g-COD) and 
overall methanogenesis (7.5 mL-air/g-COD) were initially determined using acetate and glucose as substrates, 
respectively. Subsequently, the addition of 0.5 mM oleate (a typical LCFA) increased cumulative methane pro­
duction by 22.1 % when acetate was used as the substrate after 30 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration pretreatment. 
Conversely, it decreased cumulative methane production by 17.3 % when glucose was used as the substrate after 
7.5 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration pretreatment. Additionally, the population of facultative hydrolysis microor­
ganisms, such as the genus Pseudomonas, increased by 25.7 % and 27.8 % when acetate and glucose were used as 
substrates, respectively. Furthermore, the predominant methane-producing archaea, including the genus Meth­
anosarcina, increased by 27.3 % when acetate was used as the substrate, while the genus Methanosaeta decreased 
by 65.3 % when glucose was used as the substrate. Collectively, these findings provide insights into the meth­
anogenesis pathway under optimal micro-aeration pretreatment conditions, guiding future research in this field.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a promising technology for treating 
lipid-rich organic waste (Hu et al. 2022). Theoretically, 94.8 % of lipids 
can be converted into methane during the AD process, according to the 
McCarty equation (Jeganathan et al. 2006). This makes lipids a more 
potent methane-producing substrate (1010 mL CH4/g VSS) compared to 
cellulose (379 mL CH4/g VSS), protein (496 mL CH4/g VSS) and glucose 
(351 mL CH4/g VSS) (Raposo et al. 2012). During lipid hydrolysis, long- 
chain fatty acids (LCFAs) are produced. Nevertheless, LCFAs are 
recognized as common inhibitors and pollutants in AD process 
(Elsamadony et al. 2021). Previous studies have shown that LCFAs often 
accumulate in AD reactors due to the thermodynamically unfavorable 
and energy-requiring β-oxidation pathway, which required a prolonged 
duration (Saha et al. 2019). Additionally, LCFAs can adhere to microbial 
cell membranes, disrupting microbial homeostasis and hindering the 
vital movement of methane-producing archaea (MPA) (Amha et al. 
2017, Kurade et al. 2019). To mitigate LCFA accumulation, researchers 
have explored strategies such as the supplementation of cations and 
natural adsorbents (Dereli et al. 2014, Nordell et al. 2013). However, the 
precise dosing of metal cations and the potential decomposition of 
insoluble compounds formed under thermophilic conditions can 
compromise the long-term stability of AD bioreactors (Soltan et al. 
2019). Moreover, the dosage of natural adsorbents will augment 
accompanied by LCFAs enrichment, and the adsorbents completed by 
adsorption required subsequent treatment (Reeve and Fallowfield 
2018). Therefore, it is worthwhile to investigate alternative approaches, 
such as enriching the abundance of functional microorganisms, to alle­
viate LCFA accumulation and enhance the overall efficiency of lipid-rich 
waste AD.
Previous studies have identified facultative anaerobic bacteria, such 
as genus Pseudomonas and Clostridium in phylum Firmicutes, as key

microorganisms in mitigating LCFAs inhibition (Elsamadony et al. 
2021). Recently, micro-aeration based AD system has been shown to 
effectively enrich genus Pseudomonas populations (Salome Duarte et al. 
2018). In practice, this approach not only protects strict anaerobic mi­
croorganisms including MPA, but also maintains the stability and effi­
ciency of lipid-based bio-methanation processes (Duarte et al. 2020, 
Salome Duarte et al. 2018). Furthermore, micro-aeration can enhance 
the performance of AD bioreactors in several aspects, including 
hydrogen sulfide removal, improved substrate hydrolysis efficiency and 
increased volatile fatty acids (VFAs) degradation (Nguyen and Khanal 
2018). Nevertheless, comprehensive consideration of oxygen dosage 
and aeration strategy is crucial. Excessive oxygen can negatively impact 
the activity of MPA and disrupt their anaerobic environment. 
Conversely, insufficient oxygen dosage may have a negligible influence 
on bioreactor performance (Li et al. 2024, Wu et al. 2018). A previous 
study demonstrated that micro-aeration pretreatment, specifically the 
addition of 5 mL-oxygen/g-VS during the food waste digestion process, 
maximized cumulative methane production and increased the abun­
dance of the phylum Firmicutes by 21 % compared to non-aerated 
conditions (Fu et al. 2016). Additionally, another research revealed 
that 15 mL oxygen dosage in a 1 L sequencing batch reactor resulted in a 
more than 10 % increase in cumulative methane production compared 
to non-aerated conditions, outperforming dosages of 5, 10 and 20 mL 
oxygen (Zhen et al. 2020). These findings highlight the critical role of 
micro-aeration intensity in pretreating organic waste for micro-aeration 
based AD systems. Nevertheless, optimal micro-aeration intensity can 
vary depending on the specific characteristics of the organic waste uti­
lized as substrate and its impact on the methanogenesis process. To 
determine optimal micro-aeration intensities, typical substrates such as 
acetate and glucose can be employed. In contrast, when lipid-rich 
organic waste was used as a substrate, 24 mL-oxygen/g-VS micro- 
aeration intensity can exacerbate VFAs accumulation as well as hinder 
acetate production (Rafieenia et al. 2017). Nevertheless, further 
research is needed to investigate the effects of lipid-rich organic waste 
on methanogenesis under various micro-aeration intensities. Therefore, 
oleate-rich environment is chosen as a representative lipid-rich envi­
ronment because oleate is abundant in lipid-rich wastewater (Sun et al. 
2023).
In this research, a biochemical methane potential (BMP) test was 
initially conducted using sodium acetate and glucose as substrates to 
determine the optimal micro-aeration intensity for acetoclastic and 
overall methanogenesis. Subsequently, another BMP test was performed 
to investigate the impact of oleate addition on the optimal micro- 
aeration intensity and methanogenesis process. Finally, acetoclastic 
and overall methanogenesis pathways under the optimal micro-aeration 
intensity were elucidated.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Inoculum and substrate
The seed sludge was sourced from a mesophilic (35 ± 1℃) contin­
uous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) with a 3-L working volume, operating 
at an organic loading rate of 4 g/LR d. It was acclimated to an artificial 
food waste mixture comprising fourteen kinds of food based on a pre­
vious research (Lee et al. 2008). This artificial food waste contained 
moderate amounts of pork, egg and fish, resulting in a lipid content of 
10.45 % ± 0.22 %, which can enhance microbial community’s tolerance 
to lipid-rich environments. The seed sludge exhibited the following 
characteristics: total solids (TS) of 18.04 ± 0.15 g/L, volatile solids (VS) 
of 12.18 ± 0.55 g/L, COD of 11.15 ± 0.35 g/L, and ammonia concen­
tration of 2.41 ± 0.05 g/L.
Before the formal experiment, a buffered solution was prepared to 
establish a suitable external environment for the growth of anaerobic 
microorganisms. The solution contained the following elements (mg/L): 
MgCl2⋅6H2O, 400; CaCl2⋅2H2O, 150; NH4Cl, 500; K2HPO4, 872; KH2PO4, 
680; NaHCO3, 5000; FeCl2⋅4H2O, 2; CoCl2⋅6H2O, 0.17; ZnCl2, 0.07; 
H3BO3, 0.06; MnCl2⋅4H2O, 0.611; NiCl2⋅6H2O, 0.04; CuCl2⋅2H2O, 
0.027; Na2MoO4⋅2H2O, 0.025; EDTA, 5. In addition, 4 g-COD/L acetate 
and 8 g-COD/L glucose were used as substrates respectively to supply 
carbon source for MPA during acetoclastic and overall methanogenesis.
2.2. Experimental design
The experiment was conducted in serum vial bottles with a working 
volume of 50 mL and total volume of approximately110 mL. Initially, 
each bottle was inoculated with 10 mL of seed sludge, 10 mL of buffered 
solution, 5 mL of substrate and distilled water, followed by a two-minute 
N2 purge to remove residual air. Afterwards, all bottles were compressed 
with butyl stoppers and then sealed with aluminum crimp caps. Finally, 
a small air volume was injected into each bottle to establish diverse 
micro-aeration intensities. After this procedure, the sealed bottles were 
incubated under mesophilic (35 ± 1◦C) condition in a shaker incubator 
(BS-100B, Shanghai BenTing, Inc., China) at 125 rpm.
Micro-aeration intensity and air dosage were calculated based on the 
amount of saturated dissolved oxygen and Henry’s Law. The saturated 
dissolved oxygen concentration can be calculated using the following 
formula (Zhang, 1999):
DO = p/p0*477.8/(T + 32.26).
Where p represents local barometric pressure, p0 represents standard 
barometric pressure, T represents the temperature, which is 35◦C in this 
case.
To maintain oxygen equilibrium in both the liquid phase and head­
space, a critical air volume of 3 mL was determined based on Henry’s 
Law. This volume ensures sufficient oxygen for saturation in the liquid 
phase (approximately 0.25 mL) and the headspace (approximately 0.35 
mL). To investigate the effects of varying micro-aeration intensities, four 
different air volumes (3, 6, 12 and 24 mL) were employed. These vol­
umes corresponded to micro-aeration intensities of 15, 30, 60 and 120 
mL-air/g-COD for acetoclastic methanogenesis, and 7.5, 15, 30 and 60 
mL-air/g-COD for overall methanogenesis, respectively. Additionally, a 
non-aerated control group was included. Three parallel samples were 
prepared for each micro-aeration condition. The detailed overview of 
the experimental conditions is presented in Table. 1.
As for the pivotal parameters in each serum vial bottle, the sludge VS 
content was controlled at 4 g/L. Furthermore, the oleate concentration 
was set at 0.5 mM, aligning with its previous reported IC50 value for 
traditional AD processes (Li et al. 2023, Silva et al. 2016).
2.3. Analytical methods
Biogas production was measured by a glass syringe, while biogas 
composition was analyzed via a gas chromatograph (SP-6890, Shandong 
Lunan, Inc., China). COD value was determined by COD digestion 
apparatus and a matching COD measuring instrument (HACH Loveland, 
CO, USA). TS and VS were measured according to standard methods 
(American Public Health Association, 2012). VFA samples were pre­
treated by centrifugation at 10000 rpm for 10 min and filtration through 
0.45 μm pore size filters. VFA concentrations were then detected by a gas 
chromatography (GC-2010, Shimadzu, CO, Japan). Coenzyme F420 
concentration was measured with a UV–vis spectrophotometer (P1, 
Shanghai MAPADA, Inc., China) based on the methods described in a 
previous research (Wang et al. 2020). Microbial community analysis 
involved 16S rRNA cloning and sequencing. The analysis procedure 
involved microorganism DNA extraction, polymerase chain reaction 
amplification, electrophoretic separation and fragment sequencing. The 
primers used for high-throughput sequencing were 515FmodF and 
806RmodR. Detailed procedures for 16S rRNA followed those outlined 
in a previous research (Jing et al. 2013). Significant differences (P- 
values) between acetoclastic and overall methanogenesis were calcu­
lated using Excel 2010 (Microsoft Office, 2010).

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Cumulative biogas and methane production
Fig. 1 (a) illustrates cumulative methane production over a 42-day 
period using acetate as the substrate under different micro-aeration in­
tensities, excluding the addition of 0.5 mM oleate. The results indicated 
that both 30 and 15 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration intensities promoted 
cumulative methane production by 5.2 % and 0.4 %, respectively, 
compared to non-aerated condition. Conversely, 120 mL-air/g-COD 
micro-aeration intensity hindered acetoclastic methanogenesis because 
excessive air addition contributed to more reactive oxygen species 
production exceeding microbial tolerance, which inhibited MPA meth­
anogenic activity. These findings suggest that moderate micro-aeration 
intensities could enhance acetoclastic methanogenesis efficiency, with 
30 mL-air/g-COD emerging as a potential optimal intensity.
On the other hand, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (b), while micro-aeration 
based AD system could theoretically enhance microbial tolerance, 
particularly for MPA, to oleate, the presence of oleate extended the lag 
phase of methanogenesis from 5 to 21 days, confirming its inhibitory

characteristic during AD process (Cavaleiro et al. 2016, Salome Duarte 
et al. 2018). Notably, micro-aeration intensities of 30 and 15 mL-air/g- 
COD, in the presence of 0.5 mM oleate, resulted in a 12.8 % and 3.2 % 
increase in cumulative methane production, respectively, compared to 
non-aerated condition. Meanwhile, a comparative analysis of Fig. 1 (a) 
and (b) revealed that the addition of 0.5 mM oleate consistently pro­
moted cumulative methane yield under identical aeration intensities. 
For instance, the addition of 0.5 mM oleate increased cumulative 
methane production from 355.76 ± 1.38 mL/g-COD to 388.28 ± 0.79 
mL/g-COD after 30 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration pretreatment. Further 
analysis indicated that the initial 4 g-COD/L acetate underwent com­
plete methanogenesis because the cumulative methane production 
approached the theoretical methane production potential, with the 
additional methane production attributed to the biodegradation of 0.5 
mM oleate. The COD value presented in Fig. 1 was based solely on the 
COD concentration of acetate, not the combined concentration of ace­
tate and oleate. Collectively, these findings suggest that oleate can be 
decomposed by functional hydrolysis microorganisms to supply carbon 
source for methane synthesis, even in the absence of additional external 
carbon sources.
On the other hand, Fig. 1 (c) illustrates the cumulative methane 
production using glucose as the substrate without the addition of 0.5 
mM oleate. Notably, the introduction of 0.5 mM oleate significantly 
extended the lag phase of methanogenic pathway from 1 to 21 days. In 
addition, both 7.5 and 15 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration intensities 
enhanced cumulative methane production while 60 mL-air/g-COD 
micro-aeration intensity inhibited the methanogenic process compared 
to the non-aerated condition. In specific, 7.5 and 15 mL-air/g-COD 
micro-aeration pretreatments increased cumulative methane produc­
tion by 4.8 % and 0.4 %, respectively. Based on these results, 7.5 mL-air/ 
g-COD micro-aeration intensity can be identified as the optimal one for 
overall methanogenesis. Furthermore, in the presence of 0.5 mM oleate, 
7.5 and 15 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration intensities increased cumula­
tive methane production by 3.5 % and 2.4 %, respectively. However, 
with the comparison of Fig. 1 (c) and (d), it was found that the addition 
of 0.5 mM oleate contributed to a 16.40 ± 1.90 % decrease in cumula­
tive methane production compared to oleate-free condition. This 
conclusion contrasted with the observations made when using acetate as 
the substrate. This discrepancy can be attributed to the more complex 
methanogenic pathway of glucose compared to acetate. Added oxygen 
can be consumed to promote glucose hydrolysis and acidogenesis. In the 
presence of oleate, other functional microorganisms might consume the 
initial added oxygen to hydrolyze oleate, leading to oleate accumulation 
and subsequent inhibition of MPA activity. Therefore, when considering 
micro-aeration pretreatment in oleate-rich environments, the choice of 
substrate for MPA growth should be carefully considered due to their 
varying biodegradation pathways (Oh et al. 2020).
As presented in Table. 2, the specific methanogenic activity (SMA) 
results generally aligned with the cumulative methane production 
observed in all serum vial bottles generally. A significant difference (P <
0.05) in methanogenic activity was noted between acetoclastic and 
overall methanogenesis. The SMA values indicated that the activities of 
MPA were the highest among the three parallel samples in AO3 and G2 
when acetate and glucose were used as substrates, respectively. In 
addition, when acetate was used as the substrate, the presence of oleate 
reduced methanogenesis activity under non-aerated conditions, while it 
enhanced methanogenic activity through moderate micro-aeration 
pretreatment. Conversely, when glucose was used as the substrate, the 
presence of oleate decreased overall methanogenic activity, regardless 
of aeration. This could be attributed to the relatively short hydrolysis 
duration of carbohydrates like glucose compared to lipids like oleate 
(Leung and Wang 2016). Therefore, during the glucose hydrolysis phase, 
oleate might not be sufficiently decomposed, leading to its accumulation 
around MPA and impeding its methanogenic activity. In addition, 
though the organic loading rate of the sludge used for glucose was twice 
that of acetate, it did not exceed the tolerance of the seed sludge, which 
could be stably cultivated at an organic loading rate of 4 g/LR d. This 
accounted for the decline in cumulative methane production observed in 
the presence of oleate compared to the oleate-free condition under the 
same micro-aeration intensity when glucose was used as the substrate. 
Therefore, the optimal utilization of micro-aeration pretreatment must 
be comprehensively considered when selecting diverse complex organic 
compounds utilized as substrates for MPA growth and reproduction 
under oleate-rich conditions.
3.2. SCOD value and coenzyme F420
Soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) values represent the con­
centration of dissolved organic compounds, which can serve as carbon 
sources for the growth of MPA. Generally, MPA exhibited the highest 
activity under the peak value of SCOD and the duration required to 
reach this peak value represented the lag phase of the methanogenesis 
(Zhen et al. 2020). As presented in Fig. 2, SCOD value exhibited a 
continuous downward tendency in the bottles without oleate addition. 
In contrast, samples with oleate addition showed a slight initial increase 
followed by a subsequent decrease. This suggested that organic com­
pounds, such as acetate and glucose, could be continuously utilized by 
relevant functional anaerobic microorganisms in the absence of LCFAs. 
On the other hand, LCFAs like oleate could be decomposed by faculta­
tive hydrolytic anaerobic microorganisms during the lag phase (day 1 to 
21), providing additional SCOD. Micro-aeration pretreatment could 
further enhance oleate hydrolysis, contributing to the slight increase in 
SCOD values. Subsequently, bioavailable organic compounds were 
continuously utilized by anaerobic microorganisms from day 21 to 42, 
resulting in a consecutive decrease in SCOD values. Therefore, the 
overall trends of SCOD values were consistent with the cumulative 
methane production as depicted in Fig. 1. This indicated that micro- 
aeration based AD pretreatment could promote the biodegradation of 
organic compounds under moderate micro-aeration intensities.
Though cumulative methane production stabilized after 42 days of 
cultivation, the amount of bioavailable organic compounds remaining in 
the digestion slurry after the experiment warranted further investiga­
tion. Analysis of VFA types revealed that only a small amount of acetate 
and no other types of VFA. The concentration of acetate in each serum 
vial bottle remained below 20 mg/L, regardless of the addition of oleate. 
In specific, the concentration of acetate under each experimental con­
dition ranged from 8.8 to 19.7 mg/L (equivalent to 8.2 to 18.5 mg-COD/ 
L), significantly lower than the initial supplied SCOD. Therefore, it can 
be anticipated that the supplied carbon sources, including glucose and 
acetate, had been fully utilized by functional anaerobic microorganisms. 
In addition, the absence of VFA types other than acetate in the bottles 
using acetate as the substrate indicated that oleate was decomposed into 
smaller, bioavailable organic compounds. Other fermentative microor­
ganisms utilized these compounds to produce acetate or hydrogen, 
which subsequently served as substrates for methane production.

As a typical electron carrier involved in both anabolic and catabolic 
redox reactions within the hydrogenase system, coenzyme F420 can play 
a crucial role in the growth and reproduction of hydrogen-utilizing MPA 
(Yu et al. 2023). Therefore, the concentration of coenzyme F420 could 
serve as a proxy for MPA activity (Zhang et al. 2022). In general, the 
trends in coenzyme F420 concentration observed in each serum vial 
bottle aligned with the trends in cumulative methane production. Ac­
cording to the analysis of Fig. 3, when acetate was used as the substrate, 
the bottles treated with 30 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration pretreatment 
exhibited the highest coenzyme F420 concentration (0.516 μmol/L), 
while when glucose was used as the substrate, the bottles treated with 
7.5 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration intensity showed the highest coen­
zyme F420 concentration (0.635 μmol/L). This could be attributed to the 
fact that excessive oxygen addition, such as 60 mL-air/g-COD micro- 
aeration, could inhibit MPA activity and consequently suppress coen­
zyme F420 synthesis. Conversely, inadequate air addition, such as 15 mL-

air/g-COD micro-aeration, might not significantly promote coenzyme 
F420 synthesis for acetoclastic methanogenesis. Furthermore, the addi­
tion of 0.5 mM oleate could hinder the synthesis of coenzyme F420 for 
overall methanogenesis, which can be ascribed to its incomplete 
degradation and excessive accumulation. However, it could promote the 
synthesis of coenzyme F420 for acetoclastic methanogenesis, which 
might be attributed to the additional carbon source provided by oleate 
degradation. Therefore, it was inferred that 30 mL-air/g-COD micro- 
aeration intensity was optimal for acetoclastic methanogenesis, while 
7.5 mL-air/g-COD was optimal for overall methanogenesis.
3.3. Microbial composition
According to the 16S rRNA gene sequencing results, the bacterial 
community in the seed sludge at the phylum level was primarily 
composed of Proteobacteria (29.7 %), Bacteroidota (21.2 %), Actino­
bacteriota (12.5 %), Thermotogota (10.7 %) and Firmicute (9.3 %), as 
shown in Fig. 4 (a). These phyla are commonly found in anaerobic 
bioreactors utilized for food waste treatment (Afrizal et al. 2022, Xu 
et al. 2022). After more than 35 days cultivation, the total percentage of 
Firmicute and Thermotogota achieved a significant increase from 20.0 
% to over 35.8 %, indicating that several genera within these phyla 
could survive in the provided environment, both in the presence and

absence of oleate. Nevertheless, the proportion of phylum Bacteroidota 
decreased from over 21.1 % in the seed sludge to a range of 5.1 % to 9.1 
% after the experiment. No significant changes were observed in the 
proportion of other phyla. According to previous studies, an increase in 
the abundance of Firmicute and Thermotogota had been observed in 
food waste AD bioreactor after micro-aeration pretreatment, and these 
phyla can play the role in hydrolysis and fermentation processes through 
their functional enzymes (Salome Duarte et al. 2018, Wang et al. 2022). 
Furthermore, the incremental percentage of Firmicute in the samples 
utilizing glucose as the substrate was higher than that in the samples 
utilizing acetate as the substrate, which aligned with their role in 
glucose hydrolysis process. It can be attributed to that glucose should 
undergo hydrolysis to produce acetate or carbon dioxide/hydrogen for 
subsequent methanogenesis.
On the other hand, the predominant archaea in the seed sludge at the 
genus level principally consisted of Methanosaeta (68.4 %), Meth­
anospirillum (16.2 %), and Methanoculleus (11.7 %), as depicted in Fig. 4
(b). As the most abundant archaeon in the seed sludge, Methanosaeta 
could utilize acetate as carbon source for methane synthesis via the 
acetoclastic methanogenesis pathway (Wang et al. 2024). Other pre­
dominant MPA, including Methanospirillum and Methanoculleus, could 
produce methane through hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway 
(Jain et al. 2021, Ni et al. 2022). Nevertheless, after the experiment, a 
significant increase in the abundance of the predominant MPA (genus 
Methanosarcina) was observed, especially in the bottles with oleate 
addition. This suggested that genus Methanosarcina could outcompete 
other acetate-utilizing MPA, such as Methanosaeta, under oleate-rich 
conditions. Moreover, the percentages of acetate-utilizing MPA 
including Methanosaeta and Methanosarcina and hydrogen-utilizing MPA 
including Methanospirillum and Methanoculleus remained relatively sta­
ble in the samples utilizing acetate as the substrate. Nevertheless, when 
glucose was used as the substrate, the percentage of hydrogen-utilizing 
MPA decreased while the percentage of acetate-utilizing MPA increased, 
indicating that acetate was produced in greater quantities than 
hydrogen/carbon dioxide during glucose hydrolysis.
At the genus level, genus Defluviitoga was the most abundant genus in 
all serum vial bottles. During glucose hydrolysis, Defluviitoga has been 
proved to play the role in producing small molecular organic compounds 
such as acetate, carbon dioxide and hydrogen, which serve as substrates 
for MPA (Li et al. 2019). In addition, under the optimal micro-aeration 
intensity, there was a significant increase in the abundance of genus 
Pseudomonas, a genus known to survive in both anaerobic and aerobic 
environments (Pedraz et al. 2020). This phenomenon was consistent 
with previous studies that identified genus Pseudomonas as the func­
tional anaerobic microorganism involved in mitigating LCFA accumu­
lation in micro-aeration based AD environments (Salome Duarte et al. 
2018). Other abundant genera, including Actinomyces and Alcaligenes, 
also exhibited increased abundance after the experiment. These genera 
have been previously characterized as facultative anaerobic microor­
ganisms (Corcione et al. 2018, Wang et al. 2021). Therefore, in oleate- 
rich environments with optimal micro-aeration pretreatment, certain 
genera, such as Pseudomonas, could contribute to alleviating oleate in­
hibition and ensuring the continuity of the methanogenesis pathway.
3.4. Methanogenesis pathway
Based on the aforementioned analysis, Fig. 5 illustrates the possible 
methanogenesis process under oleate-rich conditions with optimal 
micro-aeration pretreatment. In the bottles utilizing acetate as the sub­
strate with 30 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration pretreatment, oleate could 
be decomposed by functional hydrolytic microorganisms such as those 
belonging to the genus Pseudomonas. The optimal micro-aeration pre­
treatment could increase the abundance of genus Pseudomonas by 23.7 
%, thereby promoting oleate hydrolysis process. The by-products 
generated from oleate hydrolysis could be converted into acetate 
through acidogenesis, providing the substrate for acetate-utilizing MPA 
including Methanosaeta and Methanosarcina. Consequently, the abun­
dance of these microorganisms increases, contributing to enhanced 
acetoclastic methanogenesis and a 22.1 % increase in cumulative 
methane production.
On the other hand, in the bottles utilizing glucose as the substrate 
with 7.5 mL-air/g-COD pretreatment, oleate could be hydrolyzed by 
genera such as Pseudomonas, while glucose could be biodegraded by 
genera such as Defluviitoga. In specific, micro-aeration pretreatment can 
enrich the abundance of genera Pseudomonas and Defluviitoga by 27.8 % 
and 6.3 %, respectively. Nevertheless, the hydrolysis duration of glucose 
was shorter than that of oleate. This contributed to the accumulation of 
oleate around MPA before their hydrolysis. Furthermore, a higher pro­
portion of MPA transitioned to Methanosarcina rather than Meth­
anosaeta. Therefore, this hindered MPA methanogenic activity and

4. Conclusion
Micro-aeration based AD technology is a promising approach to 
mitigate LCFA accumulation and regulate biogas production, particu­
larly for pretreating lipid-rich organic waste. Micro-aeration intensity 
can be recognized as a crucial parameter in this process. This research 
demonstrated that 30 mL-air/g-COD aeration was the optimal micro- 
aeration intensity for acetoclastic methanogenesis, while 7.5 mL-air/g- 
COD aeration was optimal for overall methanogenesis in the absence 
of oleate. On the other hand, the addition of 0.5 mM oleate promoted 
acetoclastic methanogenesis by 22.1 % but inhibited overall methano­
genesis by 17.3 % under optimal micro-aeration conditions. Further­
more, this research revealed that moderate micro-aeration intensity 
accelerated the proliferation of facultative anaerobic bacteria, such as 
those belonging to the genera Pseudomonas, Actinomyces and Alcaligenes. 
Concurrently, the abundance of predominant MPA, including genus 
Methanosarcina, increased by 27.3 % during acetoclastic methano­
genesis, while the abundance of genus Methanosaeta decreased by 65.3 
% during overall methanogenesis. Therefore, appropriate micro- 
aeration intensity should be taken into systematical consideration to 
optimize methanogenesis or co-digestion efficiency. Overall, this study 
provides valuable insights into the optimal micro-aeration conditions for 
future research in this field.
